label: Person
name: Francis of Assisi
summary:
Francis of Assisi (c. 1181–1226), born Giovanni di Pietro di Bernardone, was an Italian friar and mystic who founded the Franciscan Order and became the most beloved saint in Christian history. His radical embrace of poverty, his love of nature, and his gentle charisma made him a figure who transcends religious boundaries.

The son of a wealthy cloth merchant, Francis lived as a carefree youth until a spiritual crisis during imprisonment after the Battle of Collestrada (1202). He renounced his inheritance in a dramatic public gesture, stripping naked before the bishop of Assisi and declaring God as his only father.

Francis wandered as a mendicant preacher, rebuilding ruined churches, caring for lepers, and attracting followers who became the Order of Friars Minor (Franciscans)—approved by Pope Innocent III in 1209. His 'Canticle of the Sun' (c. 1224) is the earliest major work of Italian literature.

In 1224, Francis received the stigmata—the wounds of Christ—on Mount La Verna, the first recorded instance in Christian history. He died at 44, blind and in pain, and was canonised just two years later. In 1979, Pope John Paul II declared him patron saint of ecology. As G.K. Chesterton wrote: 'He was a poet whose whole life was a poem.'

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Francis of Assisi's radical embrace of poverty and his gentle charisma inspired a global movement that continues to shape Christian history and influence Western spirituality. His legacy has had a lasting impact on art, architecture, and social justice.
